import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Euclid Numbers conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid_number)
-/

namespace EuclidNumbers

/--
The n-th Euclid number is the product of the first n prime numbers plus one.
-/
noncomputable def Euclid (n : ℕ) : ℕ := 1 + ∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, i.nth Nat.Prime

/--
It is not known whether there is an infinite number of prime Euclid numbers.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_prime_euclid_numbers : answer(sorry) ↔ {n | (Euclid n).Prime}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
It is not known whether every Euclid number is a square-free number.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem euclid_numbers_are_square_free : answer(sorry) ↔ (∀ n, Squarefree (Euclid n)) := by
  sorry

end EuclidNumbers

reformulations.difference: Lean asks for infinitely many natural-number indices n with Euclid n prime, including n = 0. The source asks for infinitely many distinct prime Euclid numbers and lists its sequence starting at n = 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Euclid is strictly increasing: each successive positive prime product is multiplied by a prime at least 2 before adding 1. Consequently, its image of a set of indices is infinite exactly when that index set is infinite. Removing the single index 0 does not affect infinitude. Proved the equivalence with `{p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ Euclid n = p}.Infinite` in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: Lean includes the empty-product index n = 0 in its universal quantifier, whereas the source's displayed Euclid sequence begins with E₁ = 3.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For positive n the definition is exactly one plus the product of the first n primes. The extra term is Euclid 0 = 2, which is squarefree. Thus universal squarefreeness over all natural indices is equivalent to universal squarefreeness over positive indices. This equivalence was proved in Lean.
